warmup.q: In a RecursiveTask, compute() splits the range into left and right, then runs left.fork(); long l = left.join(); long r = right.compute(); return l + r;. On a pool with 4 workers and 4 free cores, how much faster than one thread is it?
options: About 4 times faster, because every split forks a task
About 2 times faster, because only the top split runs in parallel
About the same speed as one thread
It deadlocks, because a worker joins its own task
warmup.why: join() right after fork() waits for the left half before the right half even exists, so the two halves of every split run one after the other. The work may hop between workers, but only one piece runs at any moment. It doesn't deadlock: a worker that joins its own task usually just runs it. Put right.compute() between the fork and the join, and the same code can keep all four workers busy. The second section measures both.

opening:
At the end of the year, the restaurant's owner wants one number: the total card fees. Each time a customer pays by card, the bank keeps a small fee. There are two million payments, and each fee takes a little arithmetic. After closing, four cooks stay to help, so the owner splits the pile four ways.

That sounds fair until one pile turns out slower, and three cooks stand around while the fourth works. A smarter kitchen lets each cook split their own pile: keep one half, and put the other half on top of their own stack. A cook who runs out takes the bottom of a busy cook's stack, where the biggest bundle waits.

That trick is called work stealing, and Java's ForkJoinPool does it for you. The trap is one line in the wrong order, which makes four cooks exactly as fast as one, with the right total.

The cooks in the last lesson waited on the phone, and these ones only compute. In this lesson, we'll split a big job, watch idle workers steal, meet parallel streams, and see one blocking call stall them all. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two million payments and four cooks who split their own piles and stole from the bottom of each other's stacks. Fork, compute, join kept four leaves running at once, and one line in the wrong order kept it to one. Parallel streams borrow the same shared team, and one cook on the phone leaves everyone waiting.

Now search your own code for parallelStream() and .parallel(). For each one, check two things: nothing inside writes to shared state, and nothing inside waits for a network, a disk or a lock.

Next, we'll take our pools into production. When something goes wrong at the busiest hour, how do you tell which pool, which thread and which request?

sections.h: One big pile, split in half until it's small: a RecursiveTask
sections.html:
Let's start with the plain version. The year's payments sit in a long[] called amounts, two million of them, each in cents. One thread, a single path of work through the program, can add them up with a loop, and for the takings, the year's total sales, that loop is the whole program. Our question is how to share such a loop among several threads without a manager handing out the work.

A ForkJoinPool, added in JDK 7 (version 7 of Java's development kit), is a thread pool, a few reused threads that run tasks for you, built for one shape of work: a big job of computation that splits itself into smaller jobs of the same kind. To fork a piece is to hand it to the pool, so that another worker can pick it up. To join it is to wait for that piece's answer. The pool's threads are called workers.

You describe the job as a RecursiveTask<V>, which returns a value, or a RecursiveAction, which doesn't. Both have one method to write, compute(), and it nearly always has this shape:

Java
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    final long[] a; final int from, to;

    SumTask(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; }

    @Override
    protected Long compute() {
        if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {                   // 1. small enough: just loop
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += a[i];
            return sum;
        }
        int mid = (from + to) >>> 1;                    // 2. split at the middle
        SumTask left = new SumTask(a, from, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, to);
        left.fork();                                    // 3. let another worker take the left half
        long r = right.compute();                       // 4. do the right half here
        return left.join() + r;                         // 5. then collect the left half
    }
}

long takings = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.length));
Kotlin
class SumTask(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() {
    override fun compute(): Long {
        if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {                   // 1. small enough: just loop
            var sum = 0L
            for (i in from until to) sum += a[i]
            return sum
        }
        val mid = (from + to) ushr 1                    // 2. split at the middle
        val left = SumTask(a, from, mid)
        val right = SumTask(a, mid, to)
        left.fork()                                     // 3. let another worker take the left half
        val r = right.compute()                         // 4. do the right half here
        return left.join() + r                          // 5. then collect the left half
    }

    companion object { const val THRESHOLD = 10_000 }
}

val takings = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.size))

Read compute() from the top. If the range holds at most THRESHOLD amounts, we just loop over it and return the sum. Otherwise we split the range at the middle into two new tasks. We fork the left one, compute the right one ourselves, and then join the left one and add the two halves. ((from + to) >>> 1 is a middle that can't overflow, even for huge arrays.) The order of those last three lines matters more than anything else here, and the next section shows why.

The threshold is the one number you have to choose: the size below which a task stops splitting and loops. Too big, and there are only a few pieces, so some workers sit idle at the end. Too small, and the cost of making and scheduling task objects eats the gain. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc, its official documentation, gives a very rough rule: a task should do more than 100 and fewer than 10,000 basic steps of computation. Then measure.

WorkStealingDemo, in the Try it below, does a heavier job than adding: it works out the card fee on each of the two million payments and totals the fees. Its fee() method does a hundred rounds of arithmetic per payment, to stand in for real fee rules. It runs once on one thread and once on a ForkJoinPool with 4 workers, and it counts the leaves, the small pieces that each worker looped over. With the default threshold of 50,000, every split halves the range until a leaf holds 31,250 payments, so there are 64 leaves:

one thread:  1,021 ms
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1    17 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2    12 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3    16 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4    19 leaves
right order, threshold 50,000: 869 ms, 7 steals, same total: true
most leaves running at the same moment: 4

Correctness first: same total: true, so the pool did exactly the work of the loop. Then speed, and here I have to be honest. This run was on a machine with 4 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time. Other programs were busy on it and kept most of the cores, so the pool was only about 1.2 times faster than one thread. The last line is the neutral referee. It counts how many leaves were running at the same moment, and it said 4. All four workers really did compute side by side. With four cores to itself, the pool could get close to four times faster. I couldn't measure that on this busy machine, so run it on yours and see how close you get.

Run it with a threshold of 500 and there are 4,096 leaves, still well spread and still fast. Run it with 1,000,000 and there are only 2 leaves, so only 2 workers ever get work, and the referee says 2.

Fork/join is for computation on data you already have in memory: summing, sorting, searching, changing every element of a big array. Its tasks should not wait for a network, a disk or a lock, for reasons the last section shows.

The demo printed one more number that deserves a question. Sixty-four leaves ended up spread across four workers, with only 7 steals. Who handed them out?

code.title: WorkStealingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Card fees on 2,000,000 payments, on a 4-worker ForkJoinPool. Args: [right|wrong] [threshold]. */ public class WorkStealingDemo { static final Map<String, LongAdder> LEAVES = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); static final AtomicInteger RUNNING = new AtomicInteger(); // leaves running right now static final AtomicInteger MOST_AT_ONCE = new AtomicInteger(); // the most that ever ran at the same moment static long fee(long amountCents) { long h = amountCents; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) h = (h * 31 + i) % 1_000_003; // stands in for real fee rules return amountCents * 29 / 1_000 + 30 + h % 2; } static final class Fees extends RecursiveTask<Long> { final long[] amounts; final int from, to, threshold; final boolean wrong; Fees(long[] amounts, int from, int to, int threshold, boolean wrong) { this.amounts = amounts; this.from = from; this.to = to; this.threshold = threshold; this.wrong = wrong; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= threshold) { LEAVES.computeIfAbsent(Thread.currentThread().getName(), k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); MOST_AT_ONCE.accumulateAndGet(RUNNING.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += fee(amounts[i]); return sum; } finally { RUNNING.decrementAndGet(); } } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; Fees left = new Fees(amounts, from, mid, threshold, wrong); Fees right = new Fees(amounts, mid, to, threshold, wrong); left.fork(); if (wrong) { long leftFees = left.join(); // waits for the left half before starting the right one return leftFees + right.compute(); } long rightFees = right.compute(); // works on the right half while the left one can be stolen return left.join() + rightFees; } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean wrong = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wrong"); int threshold = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 50_000; long[] amounts = new long[2_000_000]; for (int i = 0; i < amounts.length; i++) amounts[i] = 100 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000; long s0 = System.nanoTime(); long expected = 0; for (long a : amounts) expected += fee(a); // one thread, for comparison System.out.printf("one thread: %,d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - s0) / 1_000_000); try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4)) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long total = pool.submit(new Fees(amounts, 0, amounts.length, threshold, wrong)).join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; new TreeMap<>(LEAVES).forEach((thread, n) -> System.out.printf("%-24s %4d leaves%n", thread, n.sum())); System.out.printf("%s order, threshold %,d: %,d ms, %d steals, same total: %b%n", wrong ? "wrong" : "right", threshold, ms, pool.getStealCount(), total == expected); System.out.printf("most leaves running at the same moment: %d%n", MOST_AT_ONCE.get()); } } }

With 4 free cores, the pool can get close to 4 times faster than one thread; on a busy machine, much less. With 500 there are 4,096 leaves, and it is about as fast. With 1,000,000 there are only 2 leaves, so only 2 workers ever get work, and the last line says 2.

sections.h: Idle workers steal from the bottom: how work stealing works, and the order that keeps it parallel
sections.html:
Nobody did. A ThreadPoolExecutor, the ordinary pool from the first lessons of this track, has one shared queue, the rail that every cook takes tickets from. A ForkJoinPool gives every worker a queue of its own, a deque (say "deck"), short for double-ended queue: a line you can add to or take from at either end.

fork() pushes the task onto the top of the current worker's deque. The worker takes its own work from the top as well, so it always runs the task it forked most recently. That's the smallest piece, and its data is still in the worker's cache, the processor's small, fast copy of recently used memory.

A worker whose deque is empty becomes a thief. It picks another worker and takes the task at the bottom of that worker's deque. That's the oldest task, the one forked highest up in the splitting, so it's the biggest piece of work there is. The thief splits it on its own deque and stays busy for a long time. That's why the demo needed only 7 steals for 64 leaves. Taking work this way from another worker's deque is work stealing.

In the kitchen, each cook's deque is a personal stack of payment slips. Splitting means putting half your pile on top of your own stack and carrying on with the other half. A cook with nothing left takes the bottom bundle from a colleague's stack, the biggest one, so he won't need to come back for a while. The figure shows the same moment in code.

join() doesn't simply put the thread to sleep, either. If the forked task is still on the worker's own deque, the worker pops it and runs it right there. If a thief took it, the worker helps by running other waiting tasks until the answer is ready. So a fork/join pool needs no spare thread for each task that waits for another.

Now the order. Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, and only then join:

Java
left.fork();                    // the left half becomes stealable
long r = right.compute();       // this thread works while a thief can take the left half
return left.join() + r;
Kotlin
left.fork()                     // the left half becomes stealable
val r = right.compute()         // this thread works while a thief can take the left half
return left.join() + r

Swap the last two steps, left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute(), and the worker waits for the left half before it even starts the right one. Run the demo with wrong:

one thread:  905 ms
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1    14 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2    17 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3    17 leaves
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4    16 leaves
wrong order, threshold 50,000: 1,002 ms, 29 steals, same total: true
most leaves running at the same moment: 1

It compiles, it gives the right total, and it's a little slower than one cook. The leaves still landed on all four workers, and there were more steals than before, so at a glance the pool looks busy. The referee tells the truth: one leaf at a time.

Let's trace a single split. The worker forks the left half, so the left half sits on its deque. Then it joins the left half at once. The right half doesn't exist yet, because right.compute() comes later. So there's nothing else to do. Either the worker runs the left half itself, or a thief steals it and the worker waits. Only when the left half is done does the right half start. That happens at every level of the splitting, so the whole job runs one leaf after another, hopping between workers.

left.compute() + right.compute() is the same thing written honestly: plain sequential code with extra objects. All three versions give the right total, which is how this bug gets past code review. invokeAll(left, right) is the library's shortcut for the right order.

Fork one half, compute the other, then join. Any other order runs the halves one after the other.

You may never write a RecursiveTask yourself. You're much more likely to meet this pool through a single word: parallel.

sections.h: Parallel streams: the same pool, shared with the whole program
sections.html:
list.parallelStream(), or .parallel() on any stream, splits its source into pieces and runs them as fork/join tasks. They run on the common pool, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(): one ForkJoinPool that the whole JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs your program, shares. It's ready to use without creating anything. The thread that started the stream takes part too.

The common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 workers by default, one fewer than the cores the JVM may use, so 3 on our 4-core machine. (You can change that with a setting on the java command line, -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism.) Many users share them. Every parallel stream runs there. So does every CompletableFuture step that names no executor, the object that runs its tasks, as CompletableFuture: composing async steps showed. And since JDK 25, so do tasks scheduled on the common pool, from Scheduled executors. In the kitchen, the common pool is the one team of helpers that every part of the restaurant borrows.

Three mistakes cover most parallel stream bugs. The first is writing to shared state. SharedStateDemo sends the numbers 0 to 99,999 through a parallel stream twice. First, it adds each one to a plain ArrayList and to a shared long[] total. Then it lets the stream build the results itself, with toList() and mapToLong().sum(). Predict what the shared versions get. Here is a run of the Java version:

shared ArrayList:   50,522 of 100,000 ids, in order: false
toList():           100,000 of 100,000 ids, in order: true
shared long[] sum:  4,999,950,000
mapToLong().sum():  4,999,950,000
threads that ran the first stream: [ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-2, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3, main]

Half the ids are gone, and the shared sum came out right by pure luck. The Kotlin run straight after it was less lucky: 4,814,237,001, off by about 185 million. Both are the read-modify-write races of Race conditions: why count++ lies, where threads read a value, change it and write it back at the same moment. Four threads read the list's size, or the total, at the same moment, and some of their writes land on top of each other. Sometimes the ArrayList even throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because two threads grow its array at once.

The fix is to let the stream build the result: toList(), collect(...), sum(), reduce(...). Each thread works on its own piece, and the stream combines the pieces at the end. The last line of the output shows who did the work: the three common pool workers and main.

The second mistake is expecting order. forEach on a parallel stream runs in whatever order the threads reach the elements. toList() and forEachOrdered keep the order of the source, at some cost.

The third is too little work, or a source that splits badly. Splitting, scheduling and combining all cost time, so a stream of 1,000 cheap elements is faster sequential. How a source splits matters too. An array or an ArrayList splits in half by index, in one step, and each half can go to another worker. A LinkedList has no middle to jump to. Its Spliterator, the object that does the splitting, walks the list from the front and copies the next 1,024 elements into an array, then the next 2,048, each batch a little bigger, all on the one thread that splits. Stream.iterate and BufferedReader.lines() split badly for the same reason. Measure both versions before you keep parallel().

Never write to shared state from a parallel stream. Let the stream build the result.

Each of those mistakes stays inside your own stream. The last one reaches every other part of the program.

try.title: Collect from many threads
steps: Run SharedStateDemo. Before you do, predict the size of the shared list, and whether the shared sum is right.
Run it twice more. Which numbers change between runs, and which never do?

code.title: SharedStateDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** Collecting from a parallel stream into shared state, and the stream's own way. */ public class SharedStateDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Integer> ids = IntStream.range(0, 100_000).boxed().toList(); Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Integer> shared = new ArrayList<>(); try { ids.parallelStream().forEach(id -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); shared.add(id); // many threads, one ArrayList }); System.out.printf("shared ArrayList: %,d of %,d ids, in order: %b%n", shared.size(), ids.size(), shared.equals(ids)); } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("shared ArrayList: threw " + e); } List<Integer> collected = ids.parallelStream().map(id -> id).toList(); System.out.printf("toList(): %,d of %,d ids, in order: %b%n", collected.size(), ids.size(), collected.equals(ids)); long[] total = {0}; ids.parallelStream().forEach(id -> total[0] += id); // read, add, write from many threads long sum = ids.parallelStream().mapToLong(Integer::longValue).sum(); System.out.printf("shared long[] sum: %,d%n", total[0]); System.out.printf("mapToLong().sum(): %,d%n", sum); System.out.println("threads that ran the first stream: " + new TreeSet<>(threads)); } }

alt.title: SharedStateDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l08 import java.util.TreeSet import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap /** Collecting from a parallel stream into shared state, and the stream's own way. */ fun main() { val ids: List<Int> = (0 until 100_000).toList() val threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() val shared = ArrayList<Int>() try { ids.parallelStream().forEach { id -> threads.add(Thread.currentThread().name) shared.add(id) // many threads, one ArrayList } println("shared ArrayList: %,d of %,d ids, in order: %b".format(shared.size, ids.size, shared == ids)) } catch (e: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) { println("shared ArrayList: threw $e") } val collected = ids.parallelStream().map { it }.toList() println("toList(): %,d of %,d ids, in order: %b".format(collected.size, ids.size, collected == ids)) val total = LongArray(1) ids.parallelStream().forEach { id -> total[0] += id } // read, add, write from many threads val sum = ids.parallelStream().mapToLong { it.toLong() }.sum() println("shared long[] sum: %,d".format(total[0])) println("mapToLong().sum(): %,d".format(sum)) println("threads that ran the first stream: ${TreeSet(threads)}") }

try.expect: The shared ArrayList ends up with fewer than 100,000 ids, out of order (one run here kept 50,522), or the stream throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The shared long[] sum is usually wrong, and now and then right by luck. toList() always has all 100,000 in order, and mapToLong().sum() always prints 4,999,950,000. The thread list shows main plus the common pool workers.

refs.title: java.util.stream package: parallelism and side effects (Java SE 25 API)

aside.title: How do I measure whether parallel() helps?
aside.html: Timing a loop with System.nanoTime() is a start, but the first runs are slow while the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into fast machine code, warms up. JMH, the Java Microbenchmark Harness from the OpenJDK project, does the careful version for you. It runs your code many times, warms it up first, keeps the JIT from removing work whose result you never use, and reports each time with a margin of error. Benchmark both versions on data the size of your real input. A gain that disappears inside the margin of error isn't a gain.

sections.h: A cook on the phone: how blocking calls starve the common pool
sections.html:
A ForkJoinPool tries to keep about parallelism threads running. When one of them blocks, in Thread.sleep, a network read or a database call, the pool normally doesn't know. That worker is simply gone until the call returns.

The kitchen picture breaks here, and the break is the bug. In a real kitchen, a cook who spends ten minutes on the phone is easy to spot, and someone would share out his pile. The pool can't see that a worker is waiting.

StarvationDemo shows what that costs. It runs 16 lookups in a parallel stream, each one a 300 ms call to the slow stock service from Sizing a pool, which tells you how many of a product are left. That's four rounds of work for the 3 common pool workers plus main. As soon as all four threads are busy, another thread hands the common pool a tiny task, through supplyAsync with no executor. The task does nothing but report its thread's name:

   49 ms  blocking: common pool parallelism 3, 16 lookups of 300 ms
 1331 ms  tiny task waited 1202 ms, then ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3
 1335 ms  all lookups done

A task that takes microseconds waited 1.2 seconds, until the lookups were nearly done. Every helper in the restaurant was on hold with the stock service. In a real program, that tiny task is somebody else's request, from a part of the code that never heard of the stock service.

The fix is to keep waiting off the common pool. Run blocking calls on an executor built for waiting, such as a pool with a fixed number of threads, sized for the service you call, as Sizing a pool showed. Then combine the answers with CompletableFuture, as in the last lesson. That's the demo's io mode:

   38 ms  io: common pool parallelism 3, 16 lookups of 300 ms
  109 ms  tiny task waited 5 ms, then ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
  419 ms  all lookups done

All 16 lookups waited at the same time, so together they took little more than one lookup's 300 ms, and the tiny task waited 5 ms.

There is also a patch for code you can't move. ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker) tells the pool "this worker is about to block", and the pool may start a spare worker to keep its parallelism up. CompletableFuture uses it internally when a pool thread calls join(). In the demo's managed mode, the tiny task waited 8 ms and ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-16, one of the spares. It is still a patch. Every blocked call costs a whole platform thread, an operating system thread with its own stack, and the number of spares is capped.

You may read that a parallel stream started inside customPool.submit(...) runs on customPool. It does today, but that's how the implementation behaves, not something the specification promises. Don't build on it.

Keep blocking calls off the common pool. It belongs to the whole program.

That is the limit of this lesson's tool. Fork/join shines on computation and has nothing to offer a thread that waits. Waiting is cheap only when threads are cheap, and platform threads are not, a problem the virtual threads track takes on.

try.title: Starve the common pool
steps: Run StarvationDemo. Note how long the tiny task waits, and which thread finally runs it.
Run it with -Pargs=io, then with -Pargs=managed. Predict each time: how long do all the lookups take, and how long does the tiny task wait?

code.title: StarvationDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** Blocking stock lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ public class StarvationDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static final int PARALLELISM = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism(); static final AtomicInteger STARTED = new AtomicInteger(); static final CountDownLatch ALL_BUSY = new CountDownLatch(1); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void lookup() { if (STARTED.incrementAndGet() == PARALLELISM + 1) ALL_BUSY.countDown(); // the common pool and main are all busy sleep(300); // a call to the slow stock service } static void managedLookup() { try { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker() { boolean done; @Override public boolean block() { lookup(); done = true; return true; } @Override public boolean isReleasable() { return done; } }); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "blocking"; int lookups = (PARALLELISM + 1) * 4; // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log(mode + ": common pool parallelism " + PARALLELISM + ", " + lookups + " lookups of 300 ms"); Thread tiny = new Thread(() -> { try { ALL_BUSY.await(); // start once the lookups are under way } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long t = System.nanoTime(); String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); // a tiny task log("tiny task waited " + (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000 + " ms, then ran on " + who); }); tiny.start(); if (mode.equals("io")) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups)) { List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = IntStream.range(0, lookups) .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(StarvationDemo::lookup, io)) .toList(); calls.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); } } else { boolean managed = mode.equals("managed"); IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach(i -> { if (managed) managedLookup(); else lookup(); }); } log("all lookups done"); tiny.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: StarvationDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.stream.IntStream import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private val parallelism = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism() private val started = AtomicInteger() private val allBusy = CountDownLatch(1) private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun lookup() { if (started.incrementAndGet() == parallelism + 1) allBusy.countDown() // the common pool and main are all busy Thread.sleep(300) // a call to the slow stock service } private fun managedLookup() { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(object : ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker { var done = false override fun block(): Boolean { lookup() done = true return true } override fun isReleasable() = done }) } /** Blocking stock lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "blocking" val lookups = (parallelism + 1) * 4 // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log("$mode: common pool parallelism $parallelism, $lookups lookups of 300 ms") val tiny = thread { allBusy.await() // start once the lookups are under way val t = System.nanoTime() val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() // a tiny task log("tiny task waited ${(System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000} ms, then ran on $who") } if (mode == "io") { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups).use { io -> val calls = (0 until lookups).map { CompletableFuture.runAsync(::lookup, io) } calls.forEach { it.join() } } } else { val managed = mode == "managed" IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach { if (managed) managedLookup() else lookup() } } log("all lookups done") tiny.join() }

try.expect: In the default mode, the lookups take about 1.2 s on a 4-core machine (four rounds of 300 ms for the common pool and main), and the tiny task waits about as long, because every common pool worker is blocked. With io, the lookups take about 300 ms and the tiny task waits a few milliseconds. With managed, the pool adds spare workers, so both numbers drop again, and the tiny task runs on one of the extra threads.

compare.title: Divide and conquer: RecursiveTask vs coroutines

java.title: CountOver.java (ForkJoinPool)
java.html: class CountOver extends RecursiveTask<Integer> { final long[] a; final long limit; final int from, to; CountOver(long[] a, long limit, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.limit = limit; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Integer compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { int n = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) if (a[i] > limit) n++; return n; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; CountOver left = new CountOver(a, limit, from, mid); CountOver right = new CountOver(a, limit, mid, to); left.fork(); // stealable int r = right.compute(); // work here return left.join() + r; // then collect } } // how many payments were over 5,000.00? int big = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CountOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.length));

kotlin.title: CountOver.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun countOver(a: LongArray, limit: Long, from: Int, to: Int): Int = if (to - from <= 10_000) { (from until to).count { a[it] > limit } } else coroutineScope { val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = async { countOver(a, limit, from, mid) } // like fork() val right = countOver(a, limit, mid, to) // like compute() left.await() + right // like join() } // how many payments were over 5,000.00? val big = runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { countOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.size) }

compare.note: Kotlin can extend RecursiveTask exactly as Java does (the Kotlin WorkStealingDemo does). The coroutine version keeps the same shape and the same order rule: start the left half with async, compute the right half in place, then await. Coroutines are Kotlin's own light tasks, with a track of their own. Two things differ. Dispatchers.Default is the coroutine library's own shared pool of threads, sized to the number of cores (at least two). It isn't the common ForkJoinPool, so it doesn't compete with parallel streams. And await() suspends the coroutine instead of helping with other tasks, so the thread goes back to the dispatcher. Blocking calls are just as wrong on Dispatchers.Default as on the common pool; they belong on Dispatchers.IO.

worked.title: Speed up the year's tip report without breaking it

steps.say: The report totals the tips per waiter over the year's 400,000 sales. Someone made it parallel. Before reading on, find what breaks.
steps.code: Map<String, Long> tipsByWaiter = new HashMap<>(); sales.parallelStream().forEach(s -> tipsByWaiter.merge(s.waiter(), s.tipCents(), Long::sum)); // one HashMap, many threads

alt.html: val tipsByWaiter = HashMap<String, Long>() sales.parallelStream().forEach { s -> tipsByWaiter.merge(s.waiter, s.tipCents, Long::plus) // one HashMap, many threads }

steps.say: Many threads call merge on one HashMap. That loses updates, and a resize under several writers can corrupt the map. Let the stream build the result instead: with groupingBy, each thread fills its own small map, and the stream merges them at the end.
steps.code: // 1. computation only, and the stream owns the result Map<String, Long> tipsByWaiter = sales.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::waiter, Collectors.summingLong(Sale::tipCents)));

alt.html: // 1. computation only, and the stream owns the result val tipsByWaiter: Map<String, Long> = sales.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy({ it.waiter }, Collectors.summingLong { it.tipCents }))

steps.say: Next, someone wants each waiter's full name in the report. The names come from the staff service, a slow web service that takes 20 ms per call. Calling it inside the parallel stream would block the common pool 400,000 times. There are only 40 waiters, so look the names up after adding up, once each, on a pool built for waiting.
steps.code: // 2. waiting goes to a pool built for it, once per waiter Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> names = tipsByWaiter.keySet().stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(id -> id, id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> staff.name(id), io))); // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach((id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), tipsByWaiter.get(id)));

alt.html: // 2. waiting goes to a pool built for it, once per waiter val names = tipsByWaiter.keys.associateWith { id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ staff.name(id) }, io) } // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach { (id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), tipsByWaiter.getValue(id)) }

steps.say: Last question: is parallel() worth keeping? Adding up tips is cheap work, and for cheap work over a few hundred thousand elements, the sequential stream often wins. Time both versions on data of the real size, with a few warm-up runs or with JMH, and keep parallel() only if the numbers say so. Remember, too, that a container's CPU limit sets the size of the common pool, as Sizing a pool showed.

lab.title: Fork the year's card fees, then fix two parallel streams
steps: Meet the classes. LedgerFees is a RecursiveTask<Long> that totals the card fees on a ledger, a long array of payment amounts in cents. FeeModel works out the fee on one payment. ParallelPitfalls holds two parallel streams from the restaurant's back office, each with a bug. Run the tests: all six fail.

Write LedgerFees.compute. If to - from <= threshold, loop over the range and add up fees.feeCents(amounts[i]). Otherwise split at the middle into two new LedgerFees (use the private constructor), fork one half, compute the other, then join.

Fix ParallelPitfalls.flaggedIds, which returns the ids of the payments above a limit, in order. Keep parallelStream(), drop the shared list, and let the stream collect the ids with map(Payment::id).toList().

Fix ParallelPitfalls.stockLevels, which asks the slow stock service how many of each product are left. Start one supplyAsync(() -> stock.level(product), io) per product, collect the futures, then join them into the result map on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all six pass, then run them twice more.
hints: runsHalvesInParallel makes the first fee on each thread wait until a second thread arrives. If it times out, your two halves ran one after the other: compute the second half before you join the first.
(from + to) >>> 1 is a middle that can't overflow.

In stockLevels, create every future before you join any of them. A single stream that maps to supplyAsync and then to join handles one element at a time, so each lookup finishes before the next one starts, and stockLevelsRunsAllAtOnce times out.
lab.done: All six tests in ForkJoinTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A RecursiveTask from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a RecursiveTask<Long> that finds the largest payment of the year in a long[], with a threshold of 10,000, and the line that runs it on the common pool. Then compare. Is your compute() between the fork() and the join()?

answer.title: MaxAmount.java
answer.html: class MaxAmount extends RecursiveTask<Long> { final long[] a; final int from, to; MaxAmount(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { long max = Long.MIN_VALUE; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) max = Math.max(max, a[i]); return max; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; MaxAmount left = new MaxAmount(a, from, mid); MaxAmount right = new MaxAmount(a, mid, to); left.fork(); long r = right.compute(); return Math.max(left.join(), r); } } long max = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new MaxAmount(amounts, 0, amounts.length));

alt.title: MaxAmount.kt
alt.html: class MaxAmount(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() { override fun compute(): Long { if (to - from <= 10_000) { var max = Long.MIN_VALUE for (i in from until to) max = maxOf(max, a[i]) return max } val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = MaxAmount(a, from, mid) val right = MaxAmount(a, mid, to) left.fork() val r = right.compute() return maxOf(left.join(), r) } } val max = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(MaxAmount(amounts, 0, amounts.size))

recap: A RecursiveTask splits its range until it is below a threshold, then loops. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc suggests roughly 100 to 10,000 basic steps per leaf.
Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, then join. Joining before computing runs every split one half after the other, with the right total.
Each worker pushes and pops at the top of its own deque. Idle workers steal the oldest, biggest task from the bottom of someone else's, and join() helps instead of just waiting.
Parallel streams run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() plus the calling thread: cores minus one workers, shared with every CompletableFuture step that names no executor.
Never write to shared state from a parallel stream. Let toList(), collect, sum or reduce build the result, and measure before you keep parallel().
The limit: fork/join is for computation. Blocking calls starve the common pool, so run them on an executor built for waiting; ManagedBlocker is only a patch.

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend how work stealing keeps four workers busy on a recursive sum of the year's payments, and why left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute() gets no speed-up even though it forks.
explain.answer: Each worker has its own deque. When a task splits, it forks one half onto the top of its worker's deque and works on the other half itself. Idle workers steal from the bottom of a busy worker's deque, where the oldest and biggest piece sits, split it on their own deques, and so the work spreads across all four with only a few steals. join either runs the task itself, if nobody stole it, or helps with other work while it waits. With fork followed straight away by join, the worker waits for the left half before the right half even exists. A thief may take the left half, but the forking worker just waits for it, so the two halves of a split never overlap. Only one piece is computed at any moment, and the total time is about the same as one thread.

deeper.html:
The virtual thread scheduler, which the next track covers, is also a ForkJoinPool, a separate one from the common pool. JEP 444 describes it as a work-stealing ForkJoinPool that operates in FIFO mode, first in, first out. FIFO mode exists for tasks that are handed over and never joined, such as events or messages. You get it with the asyncMode argument of the four-argument ForkJoinPool constructor, and each worker then takes its own tasks oldest first instead of newest first.

The common pool has a few more settings, all system properties read once when the pool starts: java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism, .threadFactory, .exceptionHandler and .maximumSpares, which caps the spare threads that managedBlock can add. Calling close() or shutdown() on the common pool does nothing, so library code can't switch it off by accident.

Why does availableProcessors() - 1 make sense? Because the thread that calls invoke or starts a parallel stream works too. Seven workers plus the caller keep eight cores busy. It also means that a container limited to 2 CPUs gets a common pool of one worker, and before JDK 25 that was enough for CompletableFuture to stop using it (CompletableFuture: composing async steps).

Parallel streams don't use RecursiveTask inside. They use CountedCompleter, a ForkJoinTask that counts its pending subtasks and runs a completion action when the count reaches zero, so no thread ever waits in join(). You rarely need to write one yourself, but it's why a parallel stream can split deep trees without piling up joins.
